sentences.text: This part adds up most inputs with fixed weights, and the daytime charge counts most: it raises a typical customer's chance of leaving steadily, from under 1% at 19.07 to about 23% at 42.40 US dollars.

An international plan takes the chance from about 3% to about 20%, a voice-mail plan lowers it to under 1%, and a higher evening charge raises it steadily, from about 1% at 11.76 to about 5% at 22.57 US dollars.

More international minutes, voice-mail messages, evening minutes, night-time charge and daytime calls and a longer account each raise it steadily by about a point, and more international calls lower it, each extra call taking away about the same, from about 3% at 2 to about 2% at 8 calls.

Through it, the state moves the chance from about 3% in West Virginia to about 10% in California and Washington, about 7% in Michigan and about 6% in Montana, and down to about 1% in Vermont and under 1% in Hawaii (41 to 122 training customers per state; the full list is in the technical detail).

This part combines customer-service calls with low daytime and evening use and acts on 2378 of 4000 training customers, 249 of whom left; for the typical customer it acts on, the chance is about 1% without it and about 2% with it.

Through it, more daytime minutes lower the chance steadily up to about 194 minutes (between 160 and 235 minutes for different customers), then no further: for a typical customer from about 24% at 91 to about 2% at 352 minutes.

Customer-service calls add only from about 2 calls (between 2 and 5 calls for different customers) upwards, in an uneven way: going from 0 to 4 calls takes a typical customer from about 3% to about 9%.
A higher evening charge lowers it through this part in an uneven way, from about 6% at 11.76 to about 2% at 22.57 US dollars.

parts.original_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: logit P(churn) = -2.70 + linear_backbone + 1.646*csc_lowday_gate + 0.809*csc_lowusage_hinge - 0.067*h_day + 0.108*h_night + state offsets (-0.837*4171 + 0.029*9698 + 0.031*13306 + 0.027*16618): a purely additive combination of the children at the output sigmoid. The 24 unconnected inputs (21 states, areaCode415, nightMinutes, intlCharge) have zero effect. EVIDENCE (train): full AUC 0.905; refit L2 LR 0.843; all non-backbone children replaced by their least-squares linear fits 0.839. The gain over linear (+0.066) comes almost entirely from the two CSC x usage units: restoring either alone recovers +0.050 (776) or +0.056 (4496), together 0.905; the usage hinges and state units add nothing. They encode the known churn pattern that heavy service callers (4+ calls) churn unless their day usage is high (churn 0.87-1.0 at low day usage vs 0.14 at day z 0.5-1), together with the convex high-day-usage effect. State effects are one-hot offsets plus a state29 switch that disables 776.

parts.original_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: 4496 = relu(-1.966 - 1.843*dayMinutes - 0.859*eveCharge + g(CSC)), read out with +0.809. g is a monotone piecewise-linear function of CSC from the chain 7068 = relu(0.577*CSC-0.148) (on from 2 calls) -> 7561, 11555, 12924, 9009 (always on, so affine in 7068) plus 10362 = relu(0.933*7068-0.505) (on from 4 calls, an extra kink); g = 2.23 at 0-1 calls, 2.30 at 2, then about +0.8 per extra call (3.04 at 3, 3.88 at 4, 5.58 at 6). So 4496 is a below-average day+evening usage hinge (0.26 - 1.84*day - 0.86*eve > 0 at 0-1 calls) whose threshold and height rise with service calls. EVIDENCE (train): on for 52% of 0-call rows, 82% at 4 calls, 100% at 7+; mean logit contribution 0.74 at 0 calls, 1.56 at 4, 3.65 at 6. With the +1.92 direct dayCharge edge it makes the day effect convex: slope 1.92 above average usage, 0.43 below (and about -0.86 below z=-0.73 together with 776). Linear fit R2 0.78; linearising it alone drops train AUC 0.905 -> 0.889; restoring it alone onto the fully linearised model gains +0.056. Sensitivity: dayMinutes 1.09, eveCharge 0.51, CSC 0.29. eveCharge equals eveMinutes after z-scoring (the backbone also uses both).
